entry.title: 10 March 2023 — The ship has reached the shore

link.title: 10 March 2023 — The ship has reached the shore

entry.content:
Sent 10 March 2023. Part of Little Blue Letter.

"The ship has reached the shore"
~ Rena Lee, President of the high seas treaty negotiations
A massive win for the Ocean
Late in the evening last Saturday, the President of the Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) tasked with elaborating an Agreement to protect global Ocean biodiversity declared, “The ship has reached the shore”. After a long and winding road of more than 15 years of discussions, consensus on an Agreement to ensure the conservation and sustainable use of  biodiversity in marine areas beyond national jurisdiction (BBNJ) has finally been reached.

This is an historic moment for Ocean biodiversity, the law of the sea, the passion and dedicated community that has worked incredibly hard to get the treaty over the line, and for multilateralism in general. The Agreement sets out a process for declaring protected areas and conducting impact assessments, addresses longstanding questions regarding marine genetic resources (MGRs), and commits parties to strengthening capacity-building efforts.

For a more detailed overview, check out this blog post, setting out what is in the Agreement, what it could do, and what's happens next. You can also register for this webinar, next Wednesday, where experts will discuss the provisions, wins and losses, and next steps.

For a look inside the room where it happened, check out this lovely piece in the New Yorker.

President Rena Lee looks out at delegates to the IGC.
Credit: IISD
 
Gif of the week
Psychedelic deep-sea jellyfish.
Credit: Oceana
 
Reviving the Letter
I've brought the newsletter out of hibernation because this news is too good not to share, but you may have noticed that you haven't seen us for a while. Little Blue Letter was always a passion project, a labour of love that I could only dedicate so much time to. During covid, the number of curator sign-ups dropped, eventually to zero. (Fair enough, we were all sick of screens!)

I'd love to get it back up and running, and fulfilling it's original purpose: amplifying the voices of ocean-loving early-career researchers and connecting them to the ocean policy community. If you fancy writing an edition, please do sign-up, or forward to someone that might be interested!
Special edition by Glen Wright. Glen is a researcher studying marine governance, the high seas, and ocean energy. He is a drinker of tea, lover of the sea, and an Oxford comma user. See also: Academia Obscura: The Hidden Silly Side of Higher Education.

entry.title: 12 November 2021 — Update from COP26
entry.content:
Sent 12 November 2021. Part of Little Blue Letter.

"When the world talks about the climate crisis, the ocean crisis must be front and center in that conversation."
~ John Kerry
Update from COP26
The climate talks wrap up today, with parties wrangling over the final details of the outcome document. The good news is that the Ocean is mentioned! The draft would create an annual ocean-climate dialogue and require parties to "consider how to integrate and strengthen ocean-based action in their existing mandates and workplans". Over 100 countries signed up to a pledge to protect at least 30% of the global ocean by 2030.
Protesters at COP26 in Glasgow
© Hugo Tagholm (@HugoSAS)
  • Tuvalu’s foreign minister addressed the COP while knee-deep in the ocean to draw attention to the concerns of small island States.
  • Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador and Panama take the first step towards creating the largest transboundary marine biosphere reserve
  • Belieze has committed to spend $4 million a year and fund a $23 million marine conservation trust to protect the world's second-largest coral reef. This debt-swap model follows the pioneering efforts of the Seychelles.
  • IUCN launched a new Blue Carbon Accelerator Fund
Get involved
  • Upcoming webinar: Towards a better management of Western African Marine Resources November 23) - register here
  • Do you follow the high seas treaty negotiations? Help out researchers by filling out this survey about the impacts of covid on the negotiations
  • Sign this petition to phase out destrictive fishing practices in the EU
  • The Institute for Sustainable Development and International Relations (IDDRI) is hiring - Policy Officer, Coastal and Maritime Economy

entry.title: 23 July 2021 — Celebrating the mighty mangrove 🌱🌊🌍
entry.content:
Sent 23 July 2021. Part of Little Blue Letter.

“When the mangrove forests were not yet destroyed. It was so easy to find the wood we needed to build our houses, and we didn’t have to go very far to find mud crabs for food. But over time, the mangroves became degraded, and the crabs and fish were much harder to catch. Today, it makes me happy to see that with community reforestation efforts, life in the mangroves is slowly coming back to how it used to be.”
 
~ Evariste, Deputy President of the community association of Andimakafito village, northwest Madagascar
Celebrating the mighty mangrove 🌱🌊🌍
Mangrove forests in the Bay of Assassins, Madagascar
Garth Cripps © Blue Ventures

As the only forests that can grow in saltwater, mangroves are already an exceptional tree. They provide habitats for all manner of marine life, including fish, shrimp, crabs and megafauna, they protect shorelines against storm surges and underpin livelihoods for millions of coastal people and small-scale fishers around the world.

But the magic doesn’t stop there – mangroves are the ultimate natural solution to the climate crisis. By locking away exceptional amounts of CO₂ in their roots and sediments, these supertrees play a vital role in reducing the impacts of climate breakdown.

Not only is this good news for nature, but it’s also good news for people too. Coastal communities that live amongst the mangroves and are committed to protecting them, have the opportunity to tap into the international carbon trading market and earn an income from the sale of ‘blue carbon’ credits.

Learn more about communities in southwest Madagascar that are doing just that in this short film from Blue Ventures 👇

Watch Tahiry Honko - How a community-led conservation project delivers benefits beyond mangroves

#OceanOptimism

  • In the Sunderbans mangrove forest, spanning Eastern India and Bangladesh, young people are leading their communities to protect the ecosystem by carrying out cleanups and replanting mangroves on the most degraded islets. These young people are learning to become local stewards of the forests and passing their knowledge on to the wider community.

  • The Google Earth Engine Mangrove Mapping Methodology (GEEMMM) – a new tool which has been developed by Blue Ventures – is enabling coastal managers to map and monitor mangrove extent and change. Crucially, the GEEMMM brings an improved level of localised accuracy, creating new opportunities for coastal communities developing mangrove conservation and blue carbon projects at the local level.

Gif of the week

Scale model showing how mangrove forests protect the coast from wave erosion
Mangroves limit the effects of turbulent tides, acting as a barrier between that protects coastal communities.

Join the conversation 

  • On Wednesday 28th July, join Blue Ventures,  Mangrove Action Project (MAP), and Mikoko Pamoja for an interactive online discussion sharing learning and challenges from locally led mangrove management, called Toko telo: What does best practice in community-led mangrove management look like?. The event will kick off with a panel discussion from three mangrove experts from around the world, followed by breakout sessions in English, Bahasa Indonesia and French.

  • The Indian Ocean Rim Association is hosting a virtual meeting at the beginning of September exploring blue carbon initiatives across the Indian Ocean region. From Madagascar to Bangladesh, experts will share their experiences of engaging in and leading blue carbon initiatives.

On the Box
Revisit Sir David Attenborough’s A Perfect Planet: Oceans episode for an exploration into the deep blue. Encounter a tiny yet flamboyant cuttlefish in the reefs of Indonesia, magnificent Eden’s whales in the gulf of Thailand and curious young sharks finding refuge in the mangroves of the Bahamas.

Little Blue Letter was curated this week by Kerensa Keevill. Kerensa is Digital Communications Officer at Blue Ventures, a community-focused marine conservation organisation working across the coastal tropics.

entry.title: 29 April 2021 — Women and data collection 🎣
entry.content:
Sent 29 April 2021. Part of Little Blue Letter.

“It’s important more women get into diving and monitoring because it’s helping to challenge gender barriers. Women are strong and powerful and can do all the same things men can do. We should be treated as equals.”
~ Mima Gomez, Community Liaison Officer (Blue Ventures) based on Atauro Island, Timor-Leste

Women and data collection 🎣
Over 3 billion people worldwide depend on fish for their protein but communities often lack the data they need to make informed decisions about fisheries management and conservation. At the same time, the crucial contributions of women in small-scale fisheries have long been overlooked, resulting in less sustainable and equitable resource use. Empowering women through data collection can help solve data deficiencies while also enhancing management and conservation.
A group of women collecting data on octopus in Comoros 🐙
On the box 📺
  • Find out how Timor-Leste’s first female divemaster, Mima Gomez, is empowering women in her community to get involved in data collection.
  • Discover the positive impacts of empowering women in ocean science in the Gender and UN Ocean Decade virtual webinar series here.​
Gif of the week
Octopus are an important fisheries species for many tropical coastal communities. But did you know that some species of octopus can walk? Mind-blowing!
#OceanOptimism 🐟🐠🐡
  • The MIHARI Network and the Madagascar PHE Network have launched the FisherWomen Leadership Programme, aiming to promote leadership opportunities and increase participation of women in community fisheries management. 
  • Yet more evidence that Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) can provide benefits for regional fisheries. Populations of spiny lobsters off the coast of southern California increased both within MPAs and the adjacent waters outside the MPA boundaries.
​Join the conversation 🔊💻
  • Too Big To Ignore are hosting a small-scale fisheries open house this #WorldOceansWeek and are inviting those working with small-scale fishing communities to host a session. Find out more here.
  • Join Wilderness Markets and WWF for a webinar about their new Fisheries Improvement Fund (FIP) and learn how this new blue finance model could help make fisheries more sustainable. Register here.
Wawata Topu 🌊
Wawata Topu (Women Divers in Rasua dialect) is an award-winning documentary about four generations of fisherwomen striving to make a living in the coastal village of Adara, Water Atauro in Timor-Leste. Touching on their daily lives, this film takes a deep dive into the challenges they face in the wake of a changing world. 
Vitamin Sea
Cathedral cove - New Zealand
Credit: Marina (Unsplash)
A turtle taking a breath at the surface 
Credit: Jacob Owens (Unsplash)
A big year for our Ocean! 🌊✨
There are a number of international talks being hosted which will bring leaders together to take action for nature:
  • COP26 of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (1-12 November, Glasgow) will bring leaders together to accelerate action towards the goals of the Paris Agreement.
  • The G7 Summit (11-13 June), where climate breakdown is on the agenda.
  • COP15 of the Convention on Biological Diversity (11 October, Kunming) to decide on a post-2020 global biodiversity framework.
From the editor
  • The Marine Stewardship Council is awarding £650,000 of funding to ocean conservation and sustainability projects through its Ocean Stewardship Fund. Previous projects include reducing unwanted seabird bycatch through the use of a quirky ‘bobbing buoy’ with looming eyes on it and the development of a communications platform to enhance fishery observer safety at-sea. 
  • A look at the new generation of ocean leaders.
  • The US and New Zealand just added their support for new protected areas in east Antarctica.
  • The "Crown Jewels" of Environmental Diplomacy: Assessing the UNEP Regional Seas Programme.
Curated this week by Charlie Young and Ngaio Bowthorpe.
Charlie and Ngaio are part of the Communications team at Blue Ventures,
a community-focused marine conservation organisation working across the coastal tropics.

link.title: 11 March 2021 — The Ocean is more ancient than the mountains, and freighted with the m

entry.content:
Sent 11 March 2021. Part of Little Blue Letter.

“The Ocean is more ancient than the mountains,
and freighted with the memories and the dreams of Time."
~ H. P. Lovecraft
It's been a while! A quick note from the editor
This is the first newsletter in 2021! After the fatigue of 2020, I have unfortunately not been able to muster much energy for side projects. It seems that others are feeling the same, as nobody has signed up to curate the newsletter so far this year. Not to worry, I'll keep the project on the backburner, but as the primary purpose of the Letter is to provide a platform for young ocean leaders, there won't be so many editions in the coming months. If you want to write an edition, please feel free to sign up here.
Ocean update 
  • The new head of the World Trade Organization is pushing for members to wrap up the decades-long negotiations on the elimination of harmful fisheries subsidies.
  • The Sargasso Sea Commission has netted $3 million for projects aiming to protect the floating golden rainforest of the Atlantic.
This group of newly hatched loggerhead turtles takes refuge in the sargassum - the golden seaweed unique to the Sargasso Sea.
© WaterFrame/Alamy Stock Photo
  • The Economist World Ocean Summit just wrapped up. You can view all the sessions online. See also their recent articles on how investors can finance a sustainable ocean economy and nature-based solutions can save coral reefs.
  • New UNESCO research shows that the 50 marine sites on UNESCO World Heritage List cover at least 21% of the global area of blue carbon ecosystems - carbon assets equivalent to about 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
  • The fight for the Galápagos: race to expand reserve as fishing fleets circle
Gif of the week
© Marie Chapuis
Upcoming events
  • A webinar about China's marine spatial planning efforts.
  • An exciting symposium with new science on the contribution of ending overfishing to biodiversity and climate action.

entry.title: 17 December 2020 — Drift gillnets to be phased out in California

link.title: 17 December 2020 — Drift gillnets to be phased out in California

entry.content:
Sent 17 December 2020. Part of Little Blue Letter.

“There is a pleasure in the pathless woods,
There is a rapture on the lonely shore,
There is society, where none intrudes,
By the deep Sea, and music in its roar:
I love not Man the less, but Nature more"
~ Lord Byron
Drift gillnets to be phased out in California
The swordfish and thresher shark fishery in California will be phasing out the use of drift gillnets over the course of the next four years. Drift gillnets can be more than a mile long and reach up to 60 m (200 ft) depth from the sea surface. They are often left overnight, resulting in entanglement of various non-target species.

Around 60% of the species caught by the driftnet fishery are listed as threatened or endangered by the IUCN. The law that was passed this week aims to replace the drift gillnets with deep-set buoy gear, which will be baited for swordfish and signal to fishermen when a bite is detected. Trials of the deep-set buoy gear have shown catch consisting of over 80% swordfish compared with traditional drift gillnet gear. Under the new law, fishermen will receive a $100,000 one-off payment to surrender their nets to be destroyed, and if they choose to surrender their permit a further $10,000.
Showing the increased selectivity of the new deep-set buoy system when compared with the drift net gear.
© San Francisco Chronicle    
 
Gif of the week

Happy Holidays from the Christmas tree worms!

OceanOptimism
New species of beaked whale may have been discovered off the coast of Mexico. Three beaked whales were spotted north of San Benito Islands. Upon closer inspection of photo ID scientists realised that one of the animals did not present characteristics matching any of the described species of beaked whales. Water samples were taken to use eDNA for confirmation of the species identity.

© Sea Shepherd/CONANP 

Making Black (Women’s) Lives Matter in Marine science 
Dr Amelia Moore’s poignant and illuminating essay on the conspicuous absence of women of colour from the field of Marine Science is recommended reading for any young scientist. #BlackinMarineScienceWeek and  other initiatives have been improving the visibility of BIPOC in the field. However, we have to go much farther in order to increase accessibility. The onus and responsibility for that should not fall on the shoulders on the marginalised, it’s up to us. You can start by reading this. 
Nudibranchs that look like David Bowie
Books to inspire the next generation of marine biologists
I always struggle getting gifts for the children in my life - what does my 10-year old cousin want anyway? So, I often try to get them books, boring but rising from the fact that when I was their age the stories and books available were classic but limiting. The list compiled here showcases the best of the books available to inspire awe and understanding of the ocean. 
From the editor
Curious cases from the diatom detectives. Huge new report analysing over 3,300 Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) in Europe and their level of protection (or lack thereof) against different threats. Namibian hake fishery is second in Africa to be MSC-certified.
Diatoms, Art Forms in Nature by Ernst Haeckel | Wikimedia Commons
Little Blue Letter was curated this week by Irina Chemshirova. Irina is a PhD student at the Falkland Islands Fisheries Department and GEOMAR, Kiel. However, she rarely manages to be both places at once. Her study animal is Illex argentinus, she is investigating the delimitation of the stocks through various methods such as trace element analysis and RADseq DNA sequencing.

entry.title: 11 December 2020 — We are tied to the ocean. And when we go back to the sea, whether it i

link.title: 11 December 2020 — We are tied to the ocean. And when we go back to the sea, whether it i

entry.content:
Sent 11 December 2020. Part of Little Blue Letter.

"We are tied to the ocean.
And when we go back to the sea,
whether it is to sail or to watch,
we are going back from whence we came."
~ John F. Kennedy
A New Ocean Agenda
The High Level Panel for Sustainable Ocean Economy has launched an ambitious call to action, with the leaders of 14 countries committing to sustainably manage 100% of their waters by 2025 and to support global ocean protection targets. The announcement is a "rare show of solidarity", providing a bright spot in the Ocean super Year that never was. 
🌊  🇦🇺 🇨🇦 🇨🇱 🇫🇯 🇬🇭 🇮🇩 🇯🇲 🇯🇵 🇰🇪 🇲🇽 🇳🇦 🇳🇴 🇵🇼 🇵🇹  🌊

Many of the world's maritime powers are conspicuously absent from the Panel, e.g. France, the USA and Russia. This is not by accident: “Negotiation with that category of country isn’t all that easy... We decided to get a group where high politics wouldn’t get in the way and we could be focused on the task” - Vidar Helgesen, the former Norwegian Minister of Climate and Environment who has been a driving force behind the initiative.

By forming a "coalition of the willing", the Panel is side-stepping the incrementalism of global consensus-building and leading by example. Given that these countries manage 40% of the world's coastline, their proactive and public commitment to ocean sustainability has the potential to generate real momentum.

While the Panel does not shy away from calling for strong conservation action, they also stress need to sustainably manage all marine spaces and highlight the human dimension of ocean sustainability: increasing protein supply for a growing population, implementing nature-based solutions to limit temperature rise, and ending forced labour and other human rights abuses.
Gif of the week
Long-nosed chimaera 
Ocean update
  • Members of the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC) failed to agree measures for the management of tropical tunas (nor did they agree to maintain current measures). This leaves tropical tunas unmanaged, in clear contradiction to the IATTC's mandate, which is to... manage tropical tunas. The Global Tuna Alliance, a group of major suppliers and retailers, said it is "astonished" and "profoundly disappointed and frustrated".
  • Two new reports consider the ecology of mesopelagic fishes and the potential governance challenges of commercial exploitation. A recording of a webinar launching the reports is available here. 
Mesopelagic lanternfish
© Paul Caiger, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution

entry.title: 4 December 2020 — For civilization to survive, the human race has to remain civilized.

link.title: 4 December 2020 — For civilization to survive, the human race has to remain civilized.

entry.content:
Sent 4 December 2020. Part of Little Blue Letter.

“For civilization to survive, the human race has to remain civilized."
~ Rod Serling
Into the twilight zone
Little light reaches the depths of the Ocean's mesopelagic layer, ~150-1,000 metres below the surface. Our scientific understanding of this vast "twilight zone" remains limited, yet most of the world's fish live there, alongside a diverse range of crustaceans, cephalopods and gelatinous zooplankton ("jellies"). 
Lanternfish (myctophids), a family of about 250 species of small fish, are particularly abundant. They are a key link in marine food webs, feeding on plankton before themselves falling prey to tuna and other commercially important species.
© Paul Caiger, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute
 
Many mesopelagic organisms make a daily journey through the water column (up in the evening, down at first light). This massive migration transfers energy from the highly productive surface waters to the dark depths below and acts as a "biological pump" that locks away huge quantities of carbon.
The possibility of harvesting mesopelagic fish has been known since the 1970s but they were too hard to catch and process. (They also taste bad and contain harmful toxins.) Recent technological advancements now make it possible to fish in these waters and turn the catch into fishmeal and omega 3 oils, so interest is growing in using them for aquaculture and nutritional supplements.

Cautionary tales abound in the history of fisheries management, as humans have repeatedly fished stocks to collapse. As mesopelagic species and ecosystems play a critical role in the carbon cycle and marine food webs, mismanagement could have profound global ramifications.

In our new report, Fishing in the Twilight Zone, we tried our best to figure out how a mesopelagic fishery would be regulated under existing international rules and set out some options for strengthening the governance framework (summary blog here). The rules are messy and inadequate, and many scientists think we need a moratorium on fishing to protect the mesopelagic zone, before it's too late.

A webinar will take place next Wednesday, with leading scientists introducing the fascinating ecology of the mesopelagic zone and a discussion of the policy implications. Register here.
 
Gif of the week
 
Comb jelly
© Stefanie Shank
Ocean update
  • The High Level Panel for Sustainable Ocean Economy has launched a call to action, urging leaders to sustainably manage their waters and pushing for transformative action.
  • Two intense weeks of negotiation are expected as States try to agree on phasing out harmful fisheries subsidies: “The end is in sight for these negotiations. We have an opportunity, not to be missed, for the world to come together and exercise our collective responsibility for our precious fisheries resources, for the good of the Ocean and of the fisherfolk that rely on it” (chair of the talks, Ambassador Santiago Wills of Colombia).​
  • Negotiations on lowering shipping emissions fave failed, again.

entry.title: 27 November 2020 — Bigfin squid sightings in Australia

link.title: 27 November 2020 — Bigfin squid sightings in Australia

entry.content:
Sent 27 November 2020. Part of Little Blue Letter.

“The cure for anything is salt water: sweat, tears or the sea.
~ Isak Dinesen
Bigfin squid sightings in Australia
  • Bigfin squid (Magnapinna sp.) are one of the most cryptic animals in the deep ocean.
  • They occupy the bathypelagic zone (1,000 to 4,000 m depth) and are characterised by their unusually long arms and tentacles, and reach a total length ranging from 2 to 7 m.
  • Only a dozen sightings have been recorded worldwide, often kilometres underwater, with no adult specimens ever obtained.
  • The recent observations recorded in the Great Australian Bight are even more exciting, with multiple sightings being recorded within the same area in a short time frame.
  • This was also the first time these animals have been measured using paired lasers, giving a more accurate picture of their size.

#OceanOptimism
  • More than 100 short finned pilot whales were saved from stranding by volunteers in Sri Lanka. Although this species is known to strand in large numbers frequently, the community effort to refloat the animals took over 16 hours and was successful.
  • Tristan da Cunha has announced that 700, 000 sq. km of its waters, would be designated a Marine Protected Area (MPA), the fourth largest of its kind. The tiny island in the South Atlantic boasts with rockhopper colonies, sevengill sharks, yellow-nosed albatross and many more species that the new MPA aims to protect.

Ocean Opportunity
  • Society of Women in Marine Science is holding a virtual fall symposium on the 5th Dec 2020 and attendance is free!
  • The event aims to highlight female leaders in marine science, provide advice on career development, and facilitate mentorship in the community.
  • Register by 27th Nov 2020 i.e. today!
 
Underwater wine
  • Did you know there is such a thing as sea-water infused wine? Dating back to the ancient Greece, grapes were sunk in the sea prior to fermentation to make a sweet wine on the island of Chios.
  • Attilio Scienza and Antonio Arrighi are trying to replicate the method, producing the first 40 bottles in 2019. The result was a wine “with a scent of Mediterranean herbs and an aroma of honey and almond”.
